---
title: "Building EDI's C++ kernels once, shipping them to two languages"
description: "A short note on why EDI's model-fitting kernels are C++ underneath, and how the same source compiles into both an R package and a Python package."
date: 2026-09-16
categories: [r, python, c++, edi]
---

I'm building [EDI](https://github.com/kapelner/EDI) (Experimental Design
and Inference), an R package for randomized experimental designs — fixed
designs like blocking and optimal MILP-based allocation, and sequential
designs like matching-on-the-fly and covariate-adaptive randomization —
paired with inference procedures matched to each design and response type.
This post isn't about the statistics; it's a short engineering note on one
design decision that turned out to matter more than I expected: **every
model-fitting kernel is C++, and the same C++ source ships to two
languages.**

## Why C++ at all

EDI's whole point is that a design's assignment mechanism should carry
into its analysis — matched pairs get matched-pair inference, blocked
designs get block-aware standard errors, and so on. That means a lot of
resampling: bootstrap, jackknife, randomization tests, simulation studies
for power analysis. Every one of those re-fits a model dozens to
thousands of times. At that scale, the model fit itself is the bottleneck,
and pure R (even vectorized) loses to a compiled fit by one to three
orders of magnitude on the model families I care about — GLMs, GLMMs,
survival regressions, ordinal models. So the kernels — the actual
IRLS/Newton optimization loops — are written in C++ against
[Eigen](https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/) for the linear algebra and
[LBFGS++](https://github.com/yixuan/LBFGSpp) for optimization-based fits,
called from R via [Rcpp](https://www.rcpp.org/)/RcppEigen.

## The part I didn't expect to matter: `EDI_CORE_ONLY`

The R package needs `Rcpp::List` return types, R's RNG, R's math library
(`Rmath`) for distribution functions, and needs to run inside R's memory
model. None of that exists in a standalone C++ build. So every kernel file
in `R/EDI/src/` is written once, with the R-specific glue wrapped in
`#ifndef EDI_CORE_ONLY` guards. Compile with that macro defined, and the
same file becomes plain C++: `Eigen::VectorXd` in, `Eigen::VectorXd` out,
no R anywhere.

That's what makes [`edi_kernels`](https://pypi.org/project/edi_kernels/) —
the Python bindings — possible without a second implementation. The
Python package's CMake build `#include`s the R package's own `.cpp`/`.h`
files directly out of `R/EDI/src/`, compiles them under `EDI_CORE_ONLY`,
and wraps the result with [pybind11](https://pybind11.readthedocs.io/).
Nothing under `python/` is a copy of a kernel file — it's the same source,
a different preprocessor path. When a model-fitting bug gets fixed on the
R side, the Python bindings inherit the fix on their next build, verbatim,
because it's the same `.cpp` file.

## What this actually buys

Concretely: no "port the R fix to Python" step, no second set of
numerical bugs to find, and — since the underlying kernel is identical —
a benchmark that's honest about what it's comparing. The tradeoff is
discipline: anything R-specific has to stay inside the guard, so there's a
small CI check (`check_core_no_rcpp.sh`) that fails the build if a stray
`Rcpp::`/`SEXP` reference leaks outside it — cheap insurance against the
one mistake this whole approach is fragile to.

This is a small post — mostly a note-to-self and a pointer for anyone
building a package that's going to need more than one language's bindings
eventually. If you're in that position before you've written the kernel,
building the R-specific glue as an opt-out from day one is a lot cheaper
than retrofitting it after 100+ files exist.
